entry.gloss: the pattern of long and short sounds in time
entry.def: The pattern of durations of notes and rests in music, heard against the steady beat. Notation shows rhythm with note values and rests.

figure.staff: B4/q B4/e B4/e B4/q r/q | B4/q. B4/e B4/h |.

entry.def: The regular pulse that listeners feel and tap along to, also called the pulse. In 2/4, 3/4 and 4/4 time the beat is a quarter note; in 6/8 time it is a dotted quarter note.

entry.gloss: the grouping of beats into strong and weak
entry.def: The organization of beats into a repeating pattern of strong and weak beats, which bars and the time signature show. Meters are described by the number of beats in a bar (duple, triple, quadruple) and how each beat divides (simple or compound). Spelled metre in British English; also called time.

entry.gloss: two stacked numbers that set the meter
entry.def: Two numbers, one above the other, written after the clef and key signature. The lower number names a note value (2 for a half note, 4 for a quarter note, 8 for an eighth note) and the upper number says how many of them fill a bar: 3/4 has three quarter notes in each bar.

entry.gloss: meter whose beat divides into two
entry.def: A meter in which each beat divides into two equal parts, so the beat is a note without a dot. 2/4, 3/4 and 4/4 are simple duple, triple and quadruple meters, each with a quarter-note beat divided into two eighth notes. Called simple time in British English.

figure.staff: C5/e D5/e E5/e C5/e | D5/q G4/q |.

entry.gloss: meter whose beat divides into three
entry.def: A meter in which each beat divides into three equal parts, so the beat is a dotted note. 6/8, 9/8 and 12/8 have two, three and four dotted quarter-note beats, each divided into three eighth notes; the upper number counts the eighth notes, not the beats. Called compound time in British English.

figure.staff: C5/e D5/e E5/e F5/e E5/e D5/e | C5/q. G4/q. |.
figure.caption: Two beats in each bar, each beat a group of three eighth notes.

entry.def: A meter with two beats in each bar, strong–weak, as in 2/4, 2/2 and 6/8. Marches are often in duple meter.
A meter with three beats in each bar, strong–weak–weak, as in 3/4, 3/2 and 9/8. Waltzes and minuets are in triple meter.
A meter with four beats in each bar, as in 4/4 and 12/8. The first beat is the strongest and the third is stronger than the second and fourth.

entry.gloss: 4/4 time, written as a C-shaped sign
entry.def: Another name for 4/4 time, which can be written with a sign like a capital C instead of numbers. The sign comes from the broken circle of medieval notation, not from the word common.

entry.gloss: 2/2 time, written as a C with a vertical line
entry.def: 2/2 time: two half-note beats in each bar. It is written as the common time sign with a vertical line through it, and is also called alla breve.

entry.gloss: the first, strongest beat of a bar
entry.def: The first beat of a bar, normally the strongest. Conductors show it with a downward stroke.

entry.gloss: note or notes before the first full bar
entry.def: One or more notes before the first downbeat of a piece or phrase, written in an incomplete first bar. Also called an upbeat or a pickup. The last bar is often shortened by the same amount, so that the first and last bars together make one full bar.

figure.caption: A one-beat anacrusis in 3/4; the last bar is one beat short.

entry.gloss: stress on a weak beat or between beats
entry.def: An accent placed where the meter leads us not to expect one: on a weak beat or between beats, often with nothing new on the following strong beat.

figure.staff: C5/q D5/h C5/q | E5/e D5/q E5/e~ E5/h |.
figure.caption: The half note on the weak second beat is held through the strong third beat; in the second bar, notes begin between the beats.
